claims.text: High-temperature X-ray diffraction can effectively evaluate high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability.
HT-XRD permits in situ monitoring of phase transformations during thermal exposure.
HT-XRD permits in situ monitoring of oxidation-induced structural changes in an oxidative environment.
A material can be exposed to elevated temperature in air or controlled oxygen while in situ HT-XRD data are collected.
Temperatures above 800°C can be relevant to anticipated high-temperature service conditions.
Controlled oxygen partial pressure can be used to simulate oxidation conditions.
The evolution of XRD peaks can indicate phase transformations.
The evolution of XRD peaks can indicate the formation of oxidation products.
Heating in an oxidative environment may transform existing material phases.
Heating in an oxidative environment may form new oxide phases.
Changes in diffraction patterns recorded over time capture the temporal evolution of crystalline phases.
HT-XRD diffraction data can identify the onset of oxidation.
HT-XRD diffraction data can identify phase stability or phase transitions.
Oxidation-induced phase changes may produce shifts in diffraction-peak positions.
Oxidation-induced phase changes may alter diffraction-peak intensities or produce new peaks.
The initial diffraction pattern of an unheated, unoxidized material can serve as a reference for later measurements.
HT-XRD is most effective when phase changes are slow enough and instrument resolution is sufficient to capture intermediate phases.
Extremely rapid transformations or subsurface effects may require complementary characterization techniques.
HT-XRD may not fully capture oxidation kinetics or very transient phases.
TGA or DSC may be needed alongside HT-XRD to obtain a more complete account of oxidation kinetics.

contradictions.description: The method is proposed for assessing phase stability, but the falsification rule treats the absence of peak changes as failure. An unchanged pattern could instead be a valid observation of phase stability, so the stated null result does not necessarily falsify the method's effectiveness.

The hypothesis acknowledges that HT-XRD may miss transient or subsurface oxidation, yet the falsification rule interprets an absence of diffraction changes as falsification without excluding those acknowledged detection limitations.
